<reason>A ran a tighter strategic arc: heterogeneity and liquidity objections in the opening, sharpened in Rebuttal 1 by exposing that income-keying only trims the smallest earners rather than solving heterogeneity, and capped by a well-targeted pressure question (Q2) asking whether a direct invoice still owes the contribution. B answered honestly ("yes, owed regardless of channel"), but A then used that admission decisively in Rebuttal 2 and Closing, reframing the whole scheme as a general tax on independent income rather than a platform-specific repair, while also maintaining that restricted, earmarked accounts still create real liquidity harm for dual-covered or cash-strapped workers. B's mechanism specification (HSA-style restricted accounts) and "pay now efficiently vs. later catastrophically" framing were substantive and rhetorically strong, and B's pressure questions were also sharp, but B's Closing largely reasserted "uncovered risk is real" without directly repairing the scope/liquidity tension A had just weaponized, leaving that live clash unresolved in B's favor. B's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a minor execution cost. Overall A answered pressure more completely and controlled the final framing of the decisive clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 turning B's own Q2 answer ("owed regardless of channel") into proof that the floor is no longer a platform-specific fix but a general levy on independent contracting, a point B's Closing never squarely repaired.</best_rebuttal>
